title: Exit Desk for Orphaned Local-Marketing Assets
one_liner: A fixed-price service that finds, takes back and migrates the domain, listing, phone numbers and ad accounts locked inside shrinking legacy marketing vendors.
customer: Home-service and retail owners paying $200-1,200 a month to Yellow Pages descendants, marketing agencies and template-site hosts.
problem: Thryv's 2025 revenue was $785M and falling, with net income near $0.3M, so the vendor base is melting through price hikes, resales and shutdowns. Owners often do not own their domain, Google Business Profile admin rights, call-tracking numbers or ad accounts, and leaving means losing the phone number painted on the truck. Getting customers is still the top small-business challenge.
solution: A fixed-fee audit finds recurring vendor debits (via bank feed or bookkeeper), checks who owns each asset (WHOIS, GBP owner list, ad-account admin, tracking numbers), then executes the takeback: domain transfer, GBP ownership transfer, number port, site migration into an owner-owned stack, and contract cancellation notices. Optional monitoring alerts if a vendor re-takes control.
why_now: Legacy vendor decline is visible in public financials, AI site builders make replacement stacks cheap, and small businesses still need customers.
revenue_model: $299-799 one-time, $29/month monitoring, and referral fees from the destination stack (hosting, CRM, review tools).
non_obvious_insight: What the owner is paying for is a person who answers the phone, not leads. The exit is a control and trust problem more than a marketing problem. The bookkeeper sees the debit but has no workflow to end it.
first_30_days: Partner with 10 bookkeepers to flag legacy-vendor debits. Run 20 audits and publish a 'who owns your phone number' checklist to seed leads.

title: Do-Not-Clone Voice Registry With Inference-Time Checks
one_liner: A privacy-preserving registry that voice-cloning vendors query before creating a clone, so voice actors and narrators can block or price unauthorized cloning at the moment of input.
customer: Voice actors, audiobook narrators and podcasters (and their agents) as enrolled voices, and TTS, dubbing, audiobook and podcast-tool vendors that pay for checks and compliance logs.
problem: YouTube's likeness detection is gated by agencies and celebrity status, with no path for long-tail creators, and its removals so far are 'very small.' State laws such as Tennessee's ELVIS Act and California's digital-replica statutes create liability for cloning without consent. Vendors want a cheap way to show good faith. Detection after distribution is a losing race.
solution: Enrolled voices are stored as one-way speaker-embedding hashes. Vendors call a check API with the reference clip before creating a clone. A match requires a proof-of-consent token that carries the owner's terms (price, banned categories). Owners get logs and payouts via vendor marketplaces. Start with voice actors enrolled through agents and narrators' communities, integrated with 2-3 mid-size TTS or dubbing vendors.
why_now: Likeness laws now exist in several places, the gap for non-celebrity creators is visible, speaker-embedding models are open, and vendors selling to enterprises need a compliance line item.
revenue_model: $0.002-0.01 per check plus $1-5k/month compliance tiers for vendors, per-talent annual fees from agencies, and a marketplace take rate.
non_obvious_insight: The money is on the liability side (vendors), not the creator side, and enforcement is cheapest at input (before a clone exists) rather than at output, where the detection war is being lost.
first_30_days: Build the registry and check API prototype. Enroll 100 voice actors through two agents and a narrators' Discord. Trial the check API free with five TTS and dubbing startups, aiming for a first paid compliance tier from a dubbing vendor.

title: Defensibility Desk for GenAI Document Review
one_liner: An independent validation service that samples, blind-reviews and documents the accuracy of AI-assisted document review so litigators can defend it to opposing counsel and judges.
customer: Litigation partners and e-discovery leads at mid-size firms (25-500 lawyers), corporate litigation departments, and ALSPs and e-discovery vendors moving first-pass review to LLMs.
problem: ALSPs are consolidating around AI-enabled workflows 'engineered around human review' (Repario acquired UnitedLex on 28 Sep 2026). Review has moved from TAR to LLM classification, and opposing parties and judges will ask for proof of recall and precision. Self-validation by the team that ran the review is neither independent nor consistent, and there is no accepted protocol for LLM review.
solution: A standard protocol: statistical sampling (elusion and recall estimates with confidence intervals), blind second-pass review by a bench of reviewers, adjudication of disagreements, drift checks across model versions, and a court-ready validation declaration with optional expert testimony. It plugs into Relativity, Everlaw and DISCO by API.
why_now: Generative-AI first-pass review went mainstream in 2025-26, private equity is rolling up ALSPs on the promise of AI plus human review, and judges are scrutinizing AI use in litigation.
revenue_model: $4-20k per matter validation, $60-250k/year programs for ALSPs, and hourly expert testimony.
non_obvious_insight: AI drives first-pass review cost toward zero, which makes independent validation the billable, defensible act, and independence is what gives it evidentiary weight (like an auditor). Displaced contract reviewers are a ready workforce for it.
first_30_days: Interview 15 e-discovery counsel and design the protocol with a statistician advisor. Run three pilot validations at $3-5k on closed matters and publish the protocol as a whitepaper to build credibility.

title: Data-Center Community Benefits That Fund Rural Vets
one_liner: An intermediary that packages animal-care compacts (vet loan repayment, mobile clinics, low-cost care days, shelter energy upgrades) as community-benefit commitments for data-center developers fighting local opposition.
customer: Data-center developers and hyperscaler community-affairs teams siting campuses in rural and exurban counties, plus county officials. Payment is a program management fee on the pledged benefit package.
problem: Seven in ten Americans oppose data centers in their community (Gallup) and New York has imposed a statewide hyperscale moratorium. Delays are extremely costly (a delayed 60 MW commissioning costs about $14M a month). Typical community benefits are abstract (tax revenue, school grants). Meanwhile rural counties face a vet shortage (91,100 US vets, only about 3,100 openings a year) and vet costs are the single most visible affordability pressure for pet and livestock owners.
solution: Design and run a neutral 'Vet Access Compact' per county: loan repayment or salary top-ups for rural vets and techs, a solar-battery mobile clinic, quarterly low-cost vaccine and spay/neuter days, and shelter energy upgrades. Administer it with measurable outcomes (appointments, wait times), match it with philanthropic dollars where possible, and give the developer credible, publishable reporting. Optionally link the developer's backup power to the clinic's resilience.
why_now: Data-center opposition and moratoria surged in 2026, and electricity affordability is a midterm issue. Duffield's $250M commitment and PetSmart Charities' pledge provide matching money. New vet-professional tiers (Colorado's VPA) expand who can be funded.
revenue_model: 10-15% program design and administration fee on $1-5M multi-year packages, grant-matching and outcome-reporting retainers, and implementation fees for mobile clinics.
non_obvious_insight: Animals are one of the few bipartisan, hyper-local issues that reach every county, and a $2M program is a rounding error against a $1B campus. It pairs capital-rich, trust-poor developers with trust-rich, capital-poor local vets who also speak at public hearings.
first_30_days: Pick 3 counties with pending data-center hearings on the public calendar. Call the county veterinary association and extension office to map the gaps. Produce a one-page compact and pitch it to developers' community-affairs leads. Sell a $15-30K design study as the first paid engagement. Avoid contingent fees tied to permit outcomes.

title: Vet-Side Passport Network for Pets and Horses
one_liner: Give official veterinarians a certificate copilot that turns microchip-anchored records into error-free health certificates and a verifiable travel dossier that carriers and shippers can check before departure.
customer: Official Veterinarian practices in the UK and EU (and accredited vets in the US), plus pet and horse transport companies. Ferry, tunnel and airline operators are later payers for pre-verified manifests.
problem: Since 22 April 2026 UK-based owners must use single-entry Animal Health Certificates, 11-14 pages issued by an Official Veterinarian, instead of EU-issued passports. Vet time per certificate is heavy, the timing windows for vaccination and treatment are easy to get wrong, and a chip-number or wording error means refusal at the border. Horse shippers juggle TRACES, FEI and national passport systems separately.
solution: Software for vet practices that pulls microchip and vaccination data from practice-management systems, imports lab results, applies a country-rule engine with timing windows, pre-fills the certificate and flags errors before the vet signs. It issues the owner a portable dossier with a verifiable signature and QR code. A pre-flight checker lets shippers validate multi-animal consignments before departure.
why_now: The April 2026 EU rule change, wider TRACES digital processing, and constant UK-EU rule churn mean a maintained rules engine has recurring value. Owners are newly forced into per-trip certificates.
revenue_model: $100-190 per OV per month plus $10-20 per certificate, shipper plans from about $300 a month, and later per-manifest fees from carriers.
non_obvious_insight: The animal identity problem is already solved: microchips and horse life numbers are global standards. What is missing is trust and issuance friction, and a licensed vet is the human trust anchor. You do not need new identity infrastructure. You sell the trust anchor a better pen, and animals avoid the privacy fights that slow human wallets.
first_30_days: Recruit 10 OV practices near Dover and Folkestone, where certificate volume is highest, and 3 horse shippers. Start with the UK-to-EU Animal Health Certificate only, filling PDFs semi-manually. Charge per certificate, measure vet minutes saved and rejection rate, and publish the numbers to win the next 50 practices.

title: Neighborhood Block Wildfire Cover via HOAs
one_liner: Softer reinsurance isn't reaching homeowners, so aggregate a mitigated neighborhood into one certified risk that capital will price like a portfolio instead of 300 anonymous parcels.
customer: HOA boards and Firewise-style communities of 200-2,000 homes in wildfire states (CA, CO, UT, NM, OR) where members are being nonrenewed or pushed to FAIR plans.
problem: Nonrenewals are at records and carriers price parcel by parcel, ignoring community-level mitigation like hydrants, vegetation control, ember vents and evacuation routes. Reinsurance is softening (Jefferies expects declines through 2027) but primary policyholders see none of it.
solution: Community risk certification, drone-verified and re-certified annually, plus block placement with an MGA or coverholder writing group-rated homeowner policies backed by reinsurance or ILS capital. The HOA collects dues, funds a shared deductible reserve and enforces mitigation standards.
why_now: California passed three claims and nonrenewal bills on 2026-09-03. Cat bond issuance is a record $18.9B year to date. Softening means capital is abundant and looking for well-defined books, and nonrenewals are a midterm political flashpoint.
revenue_model: MGA commission of about 12-15% of premium, $40-$100 per home for certification, and an HOA subscription for compliance tracking.
non_obvious_insight: In a soft market capital is abundant, and what's scarce is a verifiable, homogeneous risk pool. An HOA is a ready-made legal aggregator with dues collection and enforcement powers, which solves distribution and adverse selection together.
first_30_days: Approach 20 HOA management companies and Firewise sites in California foothills and Colorado's Front Range. Offer a free community risk-certification report. Sign one pilot LOI and line up an MGA willing to quote a block program.

title: Parametric Outage Cover for Satellite Internet Users
one_liner: A $60 probe network and parametric policy that pays cash when a satellite-dependent operation loses connectivity.
customer: Mines, farms, offshore and maritime fleets, remote clinics and construction firms whose operations run on a single LEO link.
problem: Insiders treat Starlink as a utility. Operator SLAs give small credits, while the customer's loss is stopped production, idle crews or a stalled remote-operations center. Insurers avoid the risk because they have no independent measurement.
solution: Ship a probe that actively tests the customer's link and cross-checks against a global mesh of other probes. That produces tamper-resistant uptime evidence. Sell a parametric policy that pays a fixed amount per hour beyond a threshold, underwritten by an MGA and reinsurers. Add failover advice and an independent uptime scorecard for SLA negotiation.
why_now: Starlink reached 12M subscribers, and enterprise, maritime and rural operations now depend on it. A widely reported global outage in July 2025 (prior knowledge) showed correlated failure is real. Amazon and others are launching alternatives to fail over to.
revenue_model: Probe subscription $30-100 per month per site. Premium about 4-8% of annual connectivity spend once the policy launches. Data licensing to reinsurers.
non_obvious_insight: Correlated single-vendor outages are actually easy to model, and the true blocker was measurement, not appetite. A cheap independent probe network converts an 'uninsurable' risk into a priced one.
first_30_days: Build the probe on a Raspberry Pi and deploy on 50 friendly terminals from RV, farm and maritime communities. Publish an uptime dashboard. Approach two MGAs about a pilot policy and sell probe subscriptions to three fleets.

title: Drug Safety Radar for Pet Medicines
one_liner: A real-world evidence network that reads clinic notes and insurance claims to spot adverse events for newly launched pet drugs and biologics, sold to manufacturers as pharmacovigilance.
customer: Animal-health manufacturers' safety and medical-affairs teams and biotechs launching first-in-class pet therapeutics; later regulators' contractors and insurers.
problem: Adverse-event reporting in vet medicine is voluntary and sparse, and clinics rarely file forms. New launches are arriving on conditional approvals and emergency authorizations, and the post-market evidence burden is growing.
solution: Consent-based feeds from ambient-scribe notes, PIMS and insurer claims. LLMs extract exposures and events, auto-draft FDA-format adverse-event reports in one click for clinics, and run signal detection with matched comparison cohorts. First product: a fixed-fee retrospective signal report for one drug class using one insurer's de-identified claims plus 20-50 clinics.
why_now: FDA has issued 15 emergency authorizations and 3 conditional approvals for screwworm drugs as of 2026-09-03, and Loyal's LOY-002 has cleared two of three technical sections with launch possible before year-end. Ambient scribes turn notes into structured text, and IDEXX/CoVet suggests data will get walled off by incumbents.
revenue_model: $50-250K per drug program per year, per-report fees, and data licensing.
non_obvious_insight: When launches lean on conditional approvals and emergency authorizations, evidence generation becomes a cost manufacturers must pay, not a nice-to-have. The winning data source is neutral: insurers plus clinics through scribes, not the PIMS vendors who will gate access.
first_30_days: Contact safety and medical-affairs leads at 5 mid-size animal-health companies. Propose a $40K retrospective signal study on a public safety question with an insurer data partner. Release a free one-click adverse-event drafting tool to 20 clinics to seed data.

title: Permit Concierge for Rare-Plant and Reptile Sellers
one_liner: A checkout-integrated paperwork and permit service that lets hobby breeders of orchids, aroids, cacti, tarantulas and reptiles legally fill foreign orders instead of pushing buyers to the gray market.
customer: Independent rare-plant sellers (Instagram, Etsy, Facebook groups), hobby reptile/amphibian/invertebrate breeders, and small orchid/succulent nurseries doing $3k+/month that keep turning away foreign orders. Expo organizers and hobby societies (aroid, orchid, reptile expos) are a channel.
problem: All orchids and cacti, plus many other hobby species, are CITES-listed. Cross-border shipments need phytosanitary certificates, CITES export/import permits (which vary by country and by whether specimens are artificially propagated), US Lacey Act declarations, and import-inspection compliance on the EU/UK side. CITES CoP20 (Nov-Dec 2025) added listings that phase in during 2026 (verify). The paperwork is per-shipment, per-country and slow, so honest sellers refuse foreign orders, buyers turn to smugglers, and a small mistake means seizure or fines.
solution: A per-shipment service. The seller enters species and origin (propagated or wild). The system determines required documents by destination (CITES appendix and exemptions, phytosanitary certificate, carrier acceptance rules), pre-fills forms, books inspections and generates paperwork packets. It maintains a 'propagation record book' for each seller (dated photos, invoices, mother-plant records) to evidence the artificially-propagated exemption. A Shopify/Etsy plug-in quotes or blocks foreign orders with the permit fee included. A licensed customs broker/permit expeditor is the operating partner, and a wildlife-law attorney handles edge cases.
why_now: New CITES listings from CoP20 phase in through 2026 (verify). Post-Brexit UK rules and the EU Plant Health Regulation (fully applicable since Dec 2019) mean plant parcels need phytosanitary certificates, and platform and law-enforcement attention to online wildlife trade keeps rising. Rare-plant and exotic-pet hobby demand stayed high after 2020, so more sellers are hitting the cliff.
revenue_model: $89-349 per shipment. $39/month pro plan that includes the propagation record book and checkout plug-in. Referral fees from carriers/brokers. Sponsored compliance desks at hobby expos.
non_obvious_insight: Enforcement targets traffickers, but the practical legal cliff is for honest small sellers. The exemption for artificially propagated specimens means documentation of propagation is the real product: a provenance book. A seller with a clean book can charge a premium and reach EU/UK buyers competitors cannot, and a 'permit-verified' badge becomes a moat as platforms tighten.
first_30_days: Pick one lane, either CITES-listed succulents/orchids US-to-EU/UK or captive-bred reptiles. Partner with an experienced permit expeditor. Publish a free 'what paperwork does my plant need' checker to collect leads. Sign 10 sellers with pending foreign orders and process 30 shipments at about $150 each. Use the results to build templates and the propagation-book format.

title: Kennel Canary: Outbreak Surveillance for Dog Daycares
one_liner: Monthly environmental PCR swabs that give dog daycares, boarders and shelters an early-warning system and proof of due diligence.
customer: Dog daycare, boarding, grooming and training facilities (independents and franchise systems), animal shelters, and the specialty insurers that cover pet-care businesses.
problem: Canine influenza, kennel-cough pathogens and parvo outbreaks force closures, trigger owner lawsuits and tarnish reputation, and a facility can lose 20-30% of a month's revenue in one event. Facilities rely on vaccination records and owner honesty, and testing individual dogs means a vet visit ($150-300) after symptoms appear, which is hard when vets are scarce and 85% of clients decline care above $1,000.
solution: Subscription sentinel kits: pooled air-filter and surface swabs shipped to a partner lab that runs automated multiplex qPCR (CIV, CPIV, CRCoV, Bordetella, Mycoplasma cynos, Strep zooepidemicus, parvo, distemper) with 24-48 hour turnaround. Facilities get a traffic-light dashboard, outbreak playbooks (isolate, sanitize, boost vaccination), and a 'verified-clean' badge for marketing. Insurers receive premium-credit pilots. Aggregated data becomes a regional canine disease early-warning map.
why_now: Post-COVID pet ownership and return-to-office have grown daycare and boarding. Human wastewater and airborne surveillance have matured, and automated extraction plus multiplex PCR have driven per-sample costs down. Regional canine flu and respiratory outbreaks recur, and clinics have less capacity to triage.
revenue_model: $149 per month for a small facility (bi-weekly swabs), $399 per month for multi-room sites, and $50-150k per year for franchise systems. Sample cost is $20-30 at scale. Insurer-paid pilots per insured location and a $10-30k per year data subscription for vaccine makers and veterinary groups.
non_obvious_insight: What these buyers purchase is liability and reputation protection, not health testing. A sentinel result is a dated due-diligence log that insurers and lawyers value, and one avoided closure pays for a year. Pathogen surveillance built for airports and cities has never been priced for the roughly 100,000-plus US pet-care sites.
first_30_days: Partner with a university or commercial vet diagnostic lab that already has a validated respiratory multiplex PCR. Sign 5 daycares via one franchise owner or local trade group for an 8-week pilot at $99 per month. Interview two specialty insurers about credits. Publish a short 'what we found in the air' report to generate inbound interest.

title: Flooded Homeowners Meet Wetland Mitigation Buyers
one_liner: Match repeatedly flooded homeowners who want out with wetland and stream mitigation bankers who need floodplain land and can pay faster than federal buyouts.
customer: Compensatory-mitigation bankers, in-lieu-fee programs and land trusts (acquisition fee), counties and cities with repetitive-loss properties (program-management contracts), and homeowners (free, receive offers).
problem: Federal buyouts take years, and funding has become unreliable since the 2025 cancellation of BRIC and subsequent court fights. Meanwhile flood insurance premiums keep rising under Risk Rating 2.0 and repeat-flood homes are hard to sell. Mitigation bankers must buy contiguous floodplain and riparian land to earn Clean Water Act credits but usually source rural farmland by landman. They do not see suburban stream corridors lined with flooded homes as inventory.
solution: Screen NFIP repetitive-loss data, lidar and flood models and the RIBITS bank and credit ledger to find stream reaches where clusters of repeat-flood parcels adjoin high-credit-price watersheds. Run homeowner outreach and assemble willing sellers into a single package for a banker or land trust. The homes are demolished and the floodplain restored, with credits sold to permit-seeking developers and transport agencies.
why_now: Federal buyout money is slow and unpredictable, insurance repricing keeps rising, and data-center, industrial and transport permitting is driving demand for Section 404 mitigation credits. Public flood, lidar and ledger data make cluster screening possible for a small team.
revenue_model: Success fee of 2% to 3% of purchase price or $10k to $25k per assembled cluster (via a licensed real-estate partner), $2k to $5k a month screening subscription for bankers, and $50k to $150k municipal program-management contracts.
non_obvious_insight: A chain of flooded houses is exactly the restoration real estate a mitigation banker cannot otherwise get, and the funder of last resort can be a regulated compliance market rather than the taxpayer. This is a Clean Water Act compliance market, not a voluntary carbon-style offset.
first_30_days: Map 50 candidate reaches from public repetitive-loss, lidar and RIBITS data. Call 10 bankers and land trusts with a shopping list. Mail 200 homeowners on one reach. Sign a pilot with one banker and one county for program management.

title: AI-Aware E&O Cover for Solo Consultants
one_liner: A specialty insurance agency for laid-off professionals turned solo consultants whose errors-and-omissions cover may quietly exclude AI-assisted work, with premiums discounted for logged verification workflows.
customer: Solo and 2-10-person consultancies (fractional CFOs, marketing and analytics freelancers, dev contractors, HR and ops consultants) pay $400-1,500 a year in premium. The agency earns roughly 15-20% commission.
problem: Large carriers have reportedly sought AI-liability exclusions, so a freelancer who used AI on a deliverable can find a claim denied. Client contracts increasingly demand E&O plus AI-use reps. Newly independent laid-off professionals never read the policy language.
solution: A retail agency that places policies with carriers offering affirmative AI coverage (an MGA program later). A lightweight verification log (source checks, review sign-off) yields an underwriting-friendly attestation that lowers price. A contract clause checker flags indemnities, plus a template AI-use disclosure for clients.
why_now: Carrier AI-exclusion filings surfaced in late 2025, layoffs are creating a wave of new independents, and enterprise procurement now asks vendors for AI-use attestations. AI-liability startups target enterprises, not solos.
revenue_model: Commissions of 15-20%, MGA fees later, and a $10-a-month verification-log tool.
non_obvious_insight: The gap is one of underwriting information: how AI-assisted work is actually verified versus what the policy assumes. A logged verification workflow is data an insurer will pay for with lower prices. Premiums are too small for big brokers to chase, so a new insured class goes unserved.
first_30_days: Partner with a licensed E&O producer (or get licensed). Read the AI language of 10 carriers and publish a 'Does your E&O cover AI?' checker and newsletter for laid-off and freelancer communities. Bind the first 20 policies.

title: Bonded US-Only Remote Operators for Robots
one_liner: A staffing company for physical AI: background-checked, bonded, US-resident remote operators working from secure facilities on SLA-backed shifts to assist robotaxis, delivery robots and teleoperated humanoids.
customer: AV fleets, sidewalk and delivery robot operators, humanoid and mobile-manipulation startups (Series A to C) and the enterprise or health customers who demand US-based, vetted humans. The buyer is the head of operations or safety.
problem: Autonomy plateaus at 99%, and the last 1% is human labor. Waymo disclosed at a February 2026 Senate hearing that some remote assistance staff are in the Philippines, drawing political heat (Sen. Markey called it a safety issue). 1X's Neo puts a remote operator with a VR headset inside customers' homes, which is the central privacy objection. Robot startups have no staffing operation for 24/7 shift coverage, vetting, training, security controls and quality scoring.
solution: Secure operator centers (not homes) staffed with vetted US-resident operators drawn from gamers, drone pilots, veterans and military spouses. Certification per partner interface, quality scoring, audit trails and a 'named operator and session log' feature so a homeowner or hospital can see who touched what. Start with teleoperation for data collection and pilot demos, then move into live remote assistance and compliance packs.
why_now: Consumer humanoids and expanding robotaxi fleets (Waymo alone is at about 500k paid rides a week across 14 cities) make operator-hours a rapidly scaling cost. The Senate scrutiny of offshore remote assistance and the Neo privacy debate mean a 'US-only, vetted, auditable' premium is about to be demanded by regulators and enterprise buyers.
revenue_model: Billed operator-hours at $40-70/hour against a loaded cost of $25-30/hour. Premiums for compliance, security clearance and named-operator features. Setup fees for integration and certification.
non_obvious_insight: Every 10,000 robots create thousands of operator jobs, and the political fight will be about where those people sit, just as with call centers. Whoever builds the trusted, audited labor pool early owns a compliance premium that AI labs cannot easily build in-house.
first_30_days: Rent a 10-seat secured room in a mid-cost city. Buy Quest headsets and a leader-follower arm set. Recruit 15 operators from gaming and RC-drone communities and pass them through background checks. Offer 100 pilot-hours at cost-plus to 10 humanoid and delivery-robot startups who need demo and data collection help.

title: Pre-Permitted School Suites for Micro-Schools
one_liner: Master-lease vacant office and retail suites, pre-solve the change-of-use to educational occupancy, and rent furnished seats by the student to micro-school operators funded by education savings accounts.
customer: Micro-school networks and guides (per-student monthly seat rent), landlords of vacant suites (a paying tenant with no build-out risk), and ESA-funded parents underneath.
problem: Universal ESAs are minting demand: Texas alone funds $10,474 per student for 2026-27, drew 130,000+ applications in the first three weeks, and micro-school networks like Primer are opening campuses to serve it. The gate is the certificate of occupancy, not curriculum or demand. More than five children generally triggers Group E in the building code, and founders discover egress, restroom count, fire alarm and ADA gaps after signing a lease. Landlords have no standard lease and fear liability. AI-guided micro-schools need only about 25-40 sq ft per student and a few hours of adaptive software.
solution: A master-lessee that holds a portfolio of pre-engineered suites (ground floor, existing restrooms, former daycare, church, tutoring or medical use) with permit packages per jurisdiction. It subleases furnished seats month to month with a cancellation clause if ESA funding lapses, standard landlord-friendly leases and pooled insurance, plus an opening checklist and inspector relationships.
why_now: Texas ESAs go live in 2026-27 and the federal tax-credit scholarship program begins in 2027, on top of a dozen-plus states with existing ESAs. Office vacancy is 17.8%, maturity-wall landlords will take any creditworthy tenant, and the school-age population is shifting toward small-cohort, phone-light models.
revenue_model: Spread between master lease and per-seat rent (25-35% gross margin), TI financing fees, and a subscription for operators to use the permit-pack library.
non_obvious_insight: Micro-school growth is gated by a building department, not by families or teachers. The party that holds the permits, not the curriculum, owns the supply chain, and vacant offices are the wrong space until someone pre-solves the change of use.
first_30_days: Pick Texas (Austin, Dallas, Houston or San Antonio) and map 40 vacant suites with existing daycare or ground-floor restroom stock. Sign one or two 12-month master leases. Pre-sell three operators and open one site by January 2027 for spring enrollment. Get a code consultant to write a reusable permit checklist.

title: EUDR reference-number desk for downstream buyers
one_liner: An inbox-and-validator service that collects, checks and vaults EUDR reference numbers and plot GeoJSON from suppliers, sold to downstream operators and via customs brokers.
customer: Mid-size EU importers, traders and manufacturers who buy EUDR goods (wood and furniture components, coffee, cocoa, leather, rubber parts, palm derivatives) after a first operator has placed them on the market. The second channel is customs brokers and freight forwarders who white-label the desk.
problem: From 30 Dec 2026, large and medium operators and traders must comply. Downstream operators no longer file due diligence statements but must collect and keep upstream reference and verification numbers for 5 years. They cannot place goods on the market if the numbers are missing when evidently required. One guide estimates 15-30 minutes per supplier per plot for chasing, format fixes and plausibility checks, which is 'several person-weeks' at 150 suppliers, every year. Typical data faults are self-intersecting polygons from phone apps, areas off by 100x, national coordinate systems instead of WGS 84, plots outside the declared country and duplicates.
solution: A forward-to inbox and portal that (1) extracts reference and verification numbers and GeoJSON from supplier emails, PDFs, spreadsheets and invoices; (2) runs geometry checks on closed rings, self-intersection, WGS 84 with six decimals, the 4-hectare polygon rule, plot inside the declared country, duplicates and area versus tonnage plausibility; (3) auto-sends the supplier a plain-language fix request in their language, with a mobile-friendly plot-drawing link; (4) keeps a 5-year evidence vault; and (5) shows a per-purchase-order 'safe to ship or resell' status. Ship a free public GeoJSON validator first as the lead magnet.
why_now: The 30 Dec 2026 application date is fixed. The Commission's May 2026 review said the regulation will not be reopened and proposed a wider product scope through a draft delegated act, so more mid-size buyers will be pulled in. The EU TRACES NT system was reported not fully operational for the December 2025 date, so integration surprises remain.
revenue_model: SaaS tiers of EUR 79-249 per month by supplier count, plus EUR 1-3 per consignment checked. White-label to brokers at EUR 0.50-3 per declaration or a flat EUR 500-2,000 per month. Optional paid supplier-data cleanup projects.
non_obvious_insight: Filing software is crowded, but 'no DDS needed' makes downstream buyers feel safe while they inherit the messiest job: chasing numbers by email from dozens of suppliers, with a 5-year retention duty and a day-one commercial gate. As one guide puts it, 'Market access, not the fine, is the mechanism that will change behaviour first', because customers cannot resell goods without the numbers (https://www.omnia-analytics.at/en/blog/eudr-2026-operator-data-requirements, which also gives the 15-30 minute estimate and the polygon error list). Incorrect polygon format is reported as a leading cause of DDS rejection (https://www.coolset.com/academy/eudr-geolocation-requirements-how-to-collect-and-validate-gps-polygon-data-for-your-dds). Manufacturers 'do not consider themselves agricultural commodity buyers' yet inherit the duty (https://www.regilient.ai/blog/eudr-due-diligence-product-traceability-compliance). Fixing data at the supplier gives free viral distribution, because each supplier serves many buyers.
first_30_days: Build the public GeoJSON checker using open geometry libraries and rank it for searches like 'EUDR GeoJSON self-intersection error'. Pitch 3 customs brokers and 3 coffee, timber or furniture importers with a manual concierge version: they forward supplier emails and you return a cleaned register within 48 hours. Charge EUR 500 for a one-off audit of their existing supplier files. Use the audits to find the 10 most common data faults and build fix templates.

title: Member-Owned Healthspan Co-ops on the HSA Cap
one_liner: Affinity groups of 300-400 households co-own a small primary-care practice on a roughly $99-129 monthly membership that is now HSA-compatible, use group visits, and buy elite screening at pooled cash prices.
customer: Self-employed and small-business households aged 40-64 on bronze, catastrophic or high-deductible plans who already belong to a trusted group: a congregation, a 55+ community, a chamber of commerce or freelancers' guild, a farmers-market vendors' association, a large local gym.
problem: Elite prevention is sold item by item at retail prices ($200-$2,500 per test), by clinics whose upsell incentives people distrust. Direct primary care exists but rarely includes a preventive protocol and does not pool purchasing power. High deductibles leave the middle class with either a rushed annual physical or nothing between that and an emergency.
solution: A consumer co-op that hires one physician, one NP or health coach and part-time admin on a fixed monthly fee under the direct-primary-care rules. Monthly group visits (60-90 minutes, about 12 members each) cover a rotating theme (blood pressure, lipids and ApoB, sleep, strength, metabolic health) with each member's numbers on a private dashboard, plus 1:1 visits, messaging and same-week appointments. The co-op negotiates cash prices for in-office and send-out labs, coronary calcium scans, DEXA and VO2 testing (paid separately as ordinary HSA-eligible medical expenses), and members vote on which tests the protocol includes, so there is no upsell incentive. The startup provides the co-op in a box: legal templates, protocol, software, physician recruiting and a shared purchasing agreement.
why_now: Since January 1, 2026, direct primary care fees of up to $150 per month for an individual ($300 for a family) no longer disqualify someone from an HSA, and bronze and catastrophic marketplace plans became HSA-eligible, opening HSAs to roughly 7.3 million more Americans. That creates a tax-advantaged price point for exactly this product. DPC statutes exist in most states, and cash-price transparency for imaging and labs is improving.
revenue_model: Members pay the co-op $99-129 per month; the startup earns a platform and management fee of about 12-15% (roughly $15-20 per member per month) plus a $10-15k organizing fee per launch. Group purchasing agreements are structured as flat fees to stay clear of anti-kickback problems.
non_obvious_insight: The HSA rule sets a $150 ceiling that is roughly enough to fund a physician and coach if 400 households pool their membership, and the cooperative form solves the two things that block middle-class longevity medicine: trust (members own the practice and vote on the protocol) and price (pooled buying power). Group visits will not improve outcomes by themselves, as the evidence shows they are roughly equivalent to usual care, but they stretch physician time across more patients. Affinity groups already hold the trust and distribution; one founding meeting is the sales cycle.
first_30_days: Pair a burned-out primary-care physician or existing DPC doctor with one affinity group (a 400-member gym or 55+ community works). Hold a 60-minute founding meeting and collect pledge cards for 150 founding members at $99 per month. Get a state-specific legal and HSA-compliance memo on DPC and cooperative structure. Line up wholesale lab accounts and cash-price quotes from two imaging centers. Open in shared space with the first cohort within about 3-4 months.

title: Drought-to-Curtailment Forecasts for Hydro-Powered Compute
one_liner: A subscription index that forecasts 30-180 day power-curtailment risk for bitcoin miners and AI data centers on hydro-dependent grids, built from rainfall, inflow and reservoir signals.
customer: Bitcoin mining hosts and data-center operators in hydro-heavy grids (East Africa, southern Africa, Central Asia, Paraguay, Pacific Northwest), plus their lenders, equipment financiers and insurers. Operators and lenders pay.
problem: Step one: Ethiopia cut power to miners by 75% during an El Nino drought, when reservoir inflows fell about 20% in a month. Miners use over a third of a grid that is 90% hydro. Step two: every hydro grid with growing crypto and AI load faces the same triage. Step three: hosts and lenders are financing sites on 'firm cheap green power' contracts with no drought-risk model.
solution: Combine satellite rainfall, soil moisture, snowpack, ENSO outlooks and satellite-measured reservoir levels into a probability of curtailed hours per site. Map it to each grid's known dispatch rules. Backtest against Ethiopia 2026 and the 2024 Kariba (Zambia/Zimbabwe) load-shedding. Deliver a weekly dashboard and a lender-diligence report.
why_now: El Nino drought is live, WMO calls this one of the driest years for the world's rivers in 35 years, and compute loads are chasing cheap hydro. Grids have now made compute-versus-water triage an explicit decision.
revenue_model: $2-10k/month per operator portfolio, $10-30k per lender or insurer diligence report, and later an index licensed for parametric cover.
non_obvious_insight: The risk being mispriced is hydrological, not political, and the party who needs the forecast is the compute host's lender, not the grid. A dry year is a correlated credit event across every hydro-powered site.
first_30_days: Build a public-data prototype for five reservoirs. Publish a free weekly brief aimed at miners and hosting firms. Backtest and publish the Ethiopia and Kariba case studies. Pitch three hosting firms and two mining lenders for paid pilots.

title: Ritual-Accurate Wedding Data and Audits for AI
one_liner: Commission consented, styled ceremony shoots with community elders across a dozen wedding traditions, captioned by ritual stage, and sell accuracy audits and licensed datasets to image-model builders and wedding-tech companies.
customer: Generative-image model builders, stock and creative platforms with AI-licensing programs, and wedding-tech companies building AI mood boards or visualizers. Audits are $5-15k each and dataset packs are $20-150k.
problem: Image generators still get weddings wrong outside the mainstream Western template, and research on cultural bias in image models documents mis-styled Indian weddings, misidentified Korean attire and mislocalized Nigerian scenes. Web-scraped labels are worse, since 'Indian wedding' collapses Sikh, Tamil, Gujarati and Bengali ceremonies. Couples now bring AI 'inspiration' images to photographers, and wedding-tech startups embarrass themselves with visualizers that get rituals wrong in the multi-day, high-budget segments they most want. The scarce resource isn't wedding pictures, it's correctly labeled, ritual-stage-accurate images with clean releases.
solution: Rite Right runs one- and two-day ritual shoots with paid models, real officiants and community elders as advisors (no unconsented guests, so licensing is clean), photographed by working wedding pros in documentary style. Each image gets structured metadata: tradition, region, ritual stage, garment and object names, and a community-authored accuracy checklist, with model and property releases and C2PA provenance. Product one is the audit, a 'Wedding Ritual Accuracy Benchmark' (about 50 prompts per tradition) scored by elders on public and private models. Product two is licensed packs. Photographers and advisors share in license revenue.
why_now: AI-training licensing has become a real market, since Adobe and Shutterstock run contributor payout programs for training use and Getty has an OpenAI deal. Lawsuits are pushing labs toward clean, consented data, and cultural-bias evaluation of image models is an active research area. AI wedding visualizers are proliferating, and their cultural errors are viral, embarrassing and commercially costly. Audits are cheap, fast and require no dataset, so they provide first revenue while the data business builds.
revenue_model: Accuracy audits at $5-15k each (repeat quarterly as models update), dataset licensing at $20-150k per tradition pack, and rev-share to photographers and advisors. Later: a 'ritual accuracy' API for wedding-tech products.
non_obvious_insight: The photographer who has shot 40 Sikh weddings can tell in three seconds whether a laavan sequence is wrong, and that knowledge is oral, undocumented and invisible to crowd-worker labeling. What data buyers lack is not volume but the moment-by-moment ritual sequence, and only people who stand in the room at these events can supply it credibly.
first_30_days: Recruit 3 community advisors across 3 traditions from your own network. Run one styled one-day shoot on a $4-6k budget and build a 300-image sample pack with structured captions. Build a 50-prompt accuracy benchmark, score the major public image models, and publish the results as a short report to generate inbound. Email trust and safety, data and product leads at mid-size model builders and wedding-tech companies with the report and a free 10-image sample, aiming for two paid pilot audits by day 90.

title: Step-Up Basis Files for Inherited Assets
one_liner: Sell CPAs and estate lawyers a cheap, defensible date-of-death valuation packet for every inherited house or portfolio.
customer: CPAs and enrolled agents preparing 1040s and 1041s for heirs, estate attorneys, and heirs selling inherited homes or securities.
problem: The step-up in basis (IRC 1014) is the biggest tax break most families receive, but only if the heir can support date-of-death value. Below the estate-tax threshold no appraisal is required, so heirs sell years later with no valuation and risk the IRS asserting the parent's low original cost. Securities and crypto also need clean date-of-death pricing.
solution: A $150-$400 per-asset packet: houses (AVM plus retrospective appraiser sign-off), securities (date-of-death pricing), crypto, collectibles. It outputs a Basis Memo for the CPA's file, stores it, and alerts the heir when the property lists for sale.
why_now: The higher federal exemption (reported $15M) means fewer estates file a Form 706 that would have documented values. Home prices are sharply higher than a few years ago, so embedded gains are large. Boomers are the source of most transfers.
revenue_model: Per-report fees, CPA firm subscriptions, and appraiser marketplace margin.
non_obvious_insight: The tax benefit is lost through missing paperwork, not law. A small, cheap document created at death protects a large tax saving years later.
first_30_days: Sell to 15 CPA firms and 5 estate attorneys. Use an AVM API plus 3 contract appraisers per metro. Deliver in 5 business days and gather feedback on what the CPAs actually attach to returns.

title: Slop-Risk Diligence for Creator-Business Buyers
one_liner: A fixed-price quality-of-earnings report that prices the platform-policy cliff hiding inside a YouTube channel, newsletter or podcast network for sale.
customer: Search funds, micro-PE roll-ups, creator funds and revenue-based lenders acquiring channels, newsletters and podcast networks priced at roughly $200k-10M, and the brokers who sell them.
problem: Buyers price trailing-12-month revenue. But YouTube's Jul 16 clarification demonetizes generic or repetitive content and AI personas on finance, legal and health topics, Snap stopped recommending fully-AI content, and LinkedIn added a slop-report button. A channel can look healthy on the last year's statements and be one policy update from losing its income. Traditional QoE providers and listing brokers do not model this risk.
solution: A five-day diligence package: audit of how content is produced (share of AI scripts, voices and visuals, template repetition measured via embeddings, reused and stock footage), a policy-risk score against current platform rules, revenue concentration, copycat and re-post exposure, strike and claim history, and an 'earnings at risk' range with suggested earn-out triggers. Templated pipeline with analyst review.
why_now: Creator M&A and creator funds are growing (Slow Ventures' $60M creator fund, brokered channel sales), and the July 2026 policy clarifications make the next 12 months structurally different from the last 12.
revenue_model: $2.5-7.5k per report (roughly 1% of deal size), fund subscriptions for 10+ reports a year, and $500/month post-close earn-out monitoring.
non_obvious_insight: Diligence prices the past, and the AI-slop rules make the coming year differ from the past one. Policy risk is a new line in an existing budget, so no new budget is needed.
first_30_days: Pull 50 public listings from Flippa, Empire Flippers and Acquire. Publish five free teardowns, then sell $2.5k reports to buyer communities and search-fund Slack groups.

title: Neutral Baselines and Neighbor Guarantees for Data Centers
one_liner: A neutral third party installs pre-construction sensors around proposed data centers and administers a developer-funded, automatic payout guarantee to neighbors, so permit fights run on evidence.
customer: Independent and mid-size data center developers seeking 50-500 MW campus approvals in contested counties. County commissions and state regulators are a second buyer because they can make the service a permit condition. Hyperscalers with in-house community teams are not the target.
problem: Permit fights are evidence-poor. Nobody has a pre-construction baseline of well levels, night-time noise, air quality or voltage at homes, so every later complaint about dry wells or a hum can be neither proven nor disproven. Both sides fight on feelings and lawyers. Politics has turned: New York paused environmental permits for data centers of 50 MW or more in July 2026, Texas ordered its environmental regulator to stop issuing new data center permits in September 2026, and local pauses now exist in at least 14 states. A Reuters/Ipsos poll found only 14% of Americans would welcome one nearby.
solution: Baseline-in-a-Box. Over 60-90 days before the application, deploy 30-60 low-cost sensors: property-line night noise, depth and conductivity in volunteer neighbors' wells, PM2.5, night-sky brightness, and voltage sag at homes. Publish a read-only public dashboard. Have a university extension hydrogeologist and an acoustician review the methods. Escrow the data with hash-anchored timestamps so neither side can edit it. Keep monitoring for 10 years. Then add a Neighbor Guarantee: a developer-funded escrow that pays affected households automatically, like parametric crop insurance, when verified well drawdown or noise exceedances occur. No lawsuit is needed.
why_now: In 2026 the moratorium movement jumped from town boards to governors' offices (New York's executive order of July 14, Texas's TCEQ permit halt of September 21). Developers now need social license as much as megawatts, and regulators are actively drafting the frameworks that will say what evidence counts.
revenue_model: The developer pays $75-150k per site for setup, $4-10k per month for monitoring, and an 8-10% administration fee on the guarantee escrow. Counties that write the service into permit conditions create repeat demand. Later, anonymized data licensing to regulators and insurers.
non_obvious_insight: The baseline protects the developer more than the opponents. It is the only defense against future exaggerated or mistaken claims, and it turns 'trust us' into 'audit us'. Parametric payouts replace adversarial claims, which is why a rational developer buys it from a neutral party rather than opposing it.
first_30_days: Pick one county with a pending rezoning hearing (Georgia, Virginia, Indiana, Pennsylvania or Texas). Offer the developer's land agent a free 30-day pilot on 10 neighbor wells with an agricultural-extension partner. Build nodes from off-the-shelf parts at about $1.5-3k each. Present the live dashboard at the public hearing and convert that developer to a paid contract. Use the result as the case study for the next 5 developers.

title: Fair Witness: Insured Human Eyes for Remote Deals
one_liner: Heinlein's Fair Witnesses (professionals who report only what they observe) as a bonded, API-callable network that confirms the physical facts of remote transactions for people and buying agents.
customer: High-value peer-to-peer and consignment resellers (watches, pro camera gear, instruments, equipment), small landlords and property managers (move-in and move-out deposit disputes), insurers, and procurement teams or agents that need physical-world confirmation of goods received or site status.
problem: Remote deals stall on the physical world. Photos are easy to fake with generative editing, and signed-capture standards are not enough on their own (a researcher demonstrated forgery of C2PA credentials on Android in August 2026). Existing inspection services are siloed by category.
solution: Train and certify witnesses (retired inspectors, notaries) in a strict 'observe, do not infer' protocol. Capture happens on attested devices with a server-issued freshness challenge (a random code shown in frame, live geo and time nonce), 360-degree and macro video and calibrated measurements. Deliver a structured Witness Report (JSON plus signed media plus witness declaration) via API. Witnesses carry professional liability, and each report is insured up to a stated limit.
why_now: Generative editing has made photo evidence untrustworthy, while hardware-signed capture (Pixel 10 with C2PA) is only partly reliable. Agentic purchasing means software is becoming the buyer that needs a physical-world oracle, and no one supplies one with liability behind it.
revenue_model: $45-150 per visit, a monthly platform fee for API and marketplace integrations, and an insurance margin on the report guarantee.
non_obvious_insight: Camera signatures alone cannot carry trust. Trust is procedure plus a named person plus a liability plus freshness, which is exactly Heinlein's fair witness. Because witnesses give facts, not opinions, they are cheap to train (a few hours) and legally credible as fact witnesses. To avoid being another freelancer marketplace, staff is certified and insured, protocol-bound and sold through an API.
first_30_days: Recruit and certify 30 witnesses in one metro. Partner with two consignment resellers or a small-landlord association. Run 200 paid visits at about $60 and publish an anonymized accuracy and dispute-rate report.

title: Tariff Forward Curve for Section 232 Lists
one_liner: A probability feed for which HTS codes join the next Section 232 lists, with parametric hedges to follow.
customer: CFOs and sourcing heads at importers with metal-heavy lines and $20M-$1B revenue, and trade counsel. Insurers and MGAs later.
problem: Firms treat tariffs as unpredictable, so they pre-buy a year of inventory or freeze decisions. But Section 232 additions run through a public administrative pipeline of industry petitions and comment periods (the latest request for comments on 2026-08-06). Other actions carry visible dates: polysilicon at 15% with minimum import prices from 2026-12-04, and a robotics and machinery investigation still pending. Nobody publishes odds.
solution: Model each HTS-10's probability and timing of inclusion or rate change using past inclusion rounds (petitioner identity, domestic producer concentration, import share, comment volume). Update as dockets move. Deliver a dashboard, API and Slack alerts. Phase 2 is a parametric cover with an MGA or event-contract venue that pays if a heading's rate rises by a set amount within 12 months, priced off the curve.
why_now: With IEEPA gone, Section 232 is the main channel. The inclusion process is open and docketed, LLMs can read comments at scale, and event-contract and parametric markets have grown.
revenue_model: $1.5-5k a month subscription. Later, commission or spread on hedges.
non_obvious_insight: Insiders call tariffs political noise, but 232 additions follow petitioners who show up months earlier. Even 65% accuracy is worth far more than the fee to a firm deciding whether to pre-buy. Tracking current rates is crowded, but forecasting future inclusion is not.
first_30_days: Scrape BIS inclusion dockets and Federal Register notices. Hand-label the last two rounds. Publish a free weekly 'next 232 list watch' newsletter. Sign five paid pilots from importers with more than $500k of metal-derivative exposure.

title: Post-Divorce Beneficiary Cleanup for Family Lawyers
one_liner: Sell divorce attorneys a flat-fee sweep that finds and fixes stale beneficiary designations, since the will is the least important estate document.
customer: Family-law attorneys and divorce mediators or CDFAs. The initial buyer is the law firm, which adds it to the closing checklist. It expands later to advisors and benefits platforms.
problem: Most middle-class wealth passes by beneficiary designation (401(k)s, IRAs, life insurance, TOD/POD accounts), not by will. For ERISA plans the plan documents generally control even when the divorce decree says otherwise (Egelhoff v. Egelhoff, Kennedy v. Plan Administrator). Clients rarely update every form. Ex-spouses get paid, second families litigate, and the lawyer faces malpractice exposure.
solution: A 'Post-Decree Beneficiary Sweep'. The client links accounts or uploads statements. Software plus a paralegal gets each custodian's current designation, compares it to the decree, will and trust, and produces a discrepancy report. It prepares custodian-specific change forms for e-signature and tracks each until confirmed. A yearly re-audit subscription follows, triggered by life events (birth, remarriage, death).
why_now: Account aggregation and LLM extraction from messy statements and custodian PDFs now make cross-custodian paperwork cheap. Retirement balances sit at record levels, and divorce among the over-50s ('grey divorce') has risen for decades. The transfer wave is putting designation errors in the spotlight.
revenue_model: $295-$495 flat per divorce billed as a firm disbursement, $79/yr monitoring, and an enterprise license to benefits platforms and advisors at roughly $1-3 per participant per year.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone in estate planning talks about wills and trusts. The biggest mis-transfers happen through forms nobody re-reads. Divorce is the one moment when a lawyer, a deadline and malpractice fear are all in the room, so it is the cheapest place to sell an audit.
first_30_days: Sell to 10 solo and small family-law firms as a flat add-on. Process the first 20 cases manually with a paralegal and spreadsheet. Track the share of clients whose ex-spouse is still named anywhere (a hypothesis to measure) and turn that into a case study and a malpractice-avoidance pitch.

title: Common Rooms: Community-Share Buyouts of Neighborhood Bars
one_liner: A studio that helps retiring owners sell beloved bars, cafes, bookstores and cinemas to hundreds of neighbors through community-share offers, then supplies a manager and shared back office.
customer: Owners over 60 of profitable independent third-place businesses who can't find a buyer, plus neighbors who buy $100-500 shares. Commercial landlords are a third stakeholder.
problem: Boomers own most main-street businesses and many will simply close, because a qualified buyer with SBA-loan credit is rare. Communities lose their remaining third places while loneliness is a public-health issue.
solution: The UK community-pub playbook, using US tools: a Reg CF offering (up to $5M a year), an LLC or co-op with member voting, a pre-launch pledge drive to prove 300-800 neighbor investors, a professional general manager, and a shared back office (bookkeeping, permits, POS, purchasing) across all venues in the portfolio. Community shares replace acquisition debt so the business isn't forced to service a loan.
why_now: Peak-65 owners are exiting in volume, Reg CF and its platforms are mature, and retail vacancy plus loneliness make the case politically easy. In the UK, community pubs have raised about GBP 35M from 37,500+ shareholders, but the US has no equivalent operator.
revenue_model: Success fee of 3-5% of the raise, a monthly management-services contract ($1.5-3k) per venue, and vendor rebates from pooled purchasing.
non_obvious_insight: Community ownership doesn't sell returns, it sells guaranteed regulars. 500 shareholders who each show up twice a month are a customer base that exists before the doors reopen, and that is why these businesses survive at much higher rates than buyer-owned ones. The moat is the repeatable legal and marketing kit and the shared back office, not any single deal.
first_30_days: Choose one metro and phone 25 owners over 60. Find three with positive cash flow willing to sell at roughly 2-3x seller's discretionary earnings. Launch a pledge page ('would you put $250 into saving X?') to prove demand, and retain securities counsel for a templated Reg CF filing. Charge a small engagement fee up front, with the balance due on close.
